identification.summary: BLACKGEAR (also Topgear and Comnie) is a cyberespionage campaign that Trend Micro describes as active since at least 2008, mainly targeting entities in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan [S1][S3]. Its operators use the Elirks backdoor and, in later reporting, the Protux backdoor and the Marade downloader [S1][S2]. It is known for hiding command-and-control (C&C) configuration in blog, microblog and social media posts so the real C&C server can be swapped quickly [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro dates the campaign to 2008, based on the Protux backdoor its operators used [S1][S3]. Elirks was reported in 2012 as used against Taiwan [S6].
identification.notes: Trend Micro uses the name BLACKGEAR and lists Topgear and Comnie as other names [S1][S3]. Microsoft has no mapped name for this record. Unit 42 reported Elirks use in Japan in June 2016 and earlier linked an Elirks variant to the Scarlet Mimic campaign [S5]; that is a separate vendor cluster and is not merged here. Unit 42 later published related Elirks reporting under the name MILE TEA [S5].

attribution.confidence: Trend Micro stated that some limited evidence suggests the attacks may be conducted by Chinese state-sponsored actors [S2][S4]. This is a vendor assessment with limited confidence, not a government attribution.
attribution.basis: Limited evidence cited by Trend Micro; the specific indicators were not reviewed because the primary report could not be fetched [S2][S4].

objectives: Cyberespionage against public sector agencies and telecommunications and other high-technology organizations [S1][S6]. Specific collection requirements are not stated in the sources reviewed.

targeting.notes: Taiwan was the original focus, including government agencies [S6]. Trend Micro's October 2016 report said Japanese-language decoy documents and Japan-based blogging and microblogging services indicated an added focus on Japan [S1]. Later reporting describes Taiwan, South Korea and Japan as the main targets [S2][S3].

capabilities.summary: Delivery by spear-phishing email or compromised websites used for watering-hole attacks, ending in a binder that drops the malware [S1][S6]. Elirks backdoor used since at least 2012 reporting [S1][S6]. In 2018 Trend Micro described a new Protux backdoor version and the Marade downloader, delivered through spam with decoy documents or fake installers such as Adobe Flash Player; the Marade file was padded past 50 MB to evade sandboxes [S2][S4]. Encrypted C&C configurations were stored in blog and social media posts, including a Facebook post, with strings disguised as a magnet link [S2][S4]. Unit 42 observed Elirks variants using Japanese blog services across the preceding couple of years [S5].

campaigns.name: Earliest activity (Protux)
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro dates the campaign to 2008 based on the Protux backdoor used by its operators.

campaigns.name: Elirks used against Taiwan
campaigns.summary: Elirks was reported as used to target Taiwan, including government agencies.

campaigns.name: Elirks variants in Japan (Unit 42)
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 reported Elirks variants using Japanese blog services and tied a recent attack on a Japanese business that involved PlugX and Elirks to earlier Elirks activity. Unit 42 treats this under its own cluster naming.

campaigns.name: Expansion to Japan
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro reported BLACKGEAR using Japanese-language decoy documents and Japan-based blogging and microblogging services for C&C.

campaigns.name: Resurgence with Protux, Marade and social media C&C
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro described a new operation beginning in early July 2018 using a new Protux version and the Marade downloader, with C&C configuration hidden in blog and social media posts including Facebook.

diamond.adversary: Unattributed operators; Trend Micro cites limited evidence of possible Chinese state sponsorship [S2][S4].
diamond.capability: Elirks, Protux and Marade; binder-based droppers; spear-phishing, watering holes and fake installers; oversized files to evade sandboxes [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: C&C addresses held in encrypted form in blog, microblog and social media posts (including Japan-based services and Facebook), letting operators change servers by editing a post [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.victim: Public sector, telecommunications and other high-technology organizations in Taiwan, Japan and South Korea [S1][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Regional intelligence collection in East Asia; the sources reviewed do not state requirements beyond espionage [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Email and web browsing by government and technology staff, and reliance on commodity blogging and social media services that defenders usually allow, which hides C&C lookups [S2][S4].

gaps: The primary Trend Micro reports (October 2016 and July 2018) could not be fetched; facts come from search excerpts and secondary coverage and should be verified against the originals [S1][S2].
Basis for the limited Chinese state-sponsorship assessment is not available; no government attribution was found.
Relationship to the Scarlet Mimic and MILE TEA clusters named by Unit 42 (shared Elirks malware and infrastructure) is unresolved and not merged here [S5].
Publication dates for S3, S4 and S6 are approximate (month taken from search results).
No victim counts, named victims or activity after 2018 were found.
No MITRE ATT&CK group, no Microsoft name and no US government reporting were identified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Government and telecom or high-technology networks in Taiwan, Japan and South Korea, with email gateways and web proxies as key terrain [S1][S3]. STEP 2: Commodity blog and social media platforms are allowed by default on most networks, giving the actor a hard-to-block C&C channel [S2]. STEP 3: Spear-phishing or watering hole, then binder, then Elirks, Protux or Marade, then C&C fetched from a social media post [S1][S2][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued low-volume espionage against regional government and telecom targets with rotating C&C posts. MDCOA is use of telecom or government footholds in an allied partner nation for collection during a regional crisis. Candidate indicators: unusually large (50 MB+) executables from email, hosts querying blog or social media pages with encoded strings (including magnet-link style text), and fake software installers [S2][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track regional partner-nation compromise reporting, since Taiwan, Japan and South Korea are named targets [S3]. (2) Authorities: partner-network defense typically needs host-nation consent or sharing channels; plan indicator sharing through established agreements. (3) Mission assurance: restrict personal social media and blog access from mission systems or log it, and sandbox large email attachments [S2][S4]. (4) Coordination: confidence in sponsorship is low, so share indicators without asserting attribution [S2].

provenance.importedSummary: BLACKGEAR is an espionage campaign which has targeted users in Taiwan for many years. Multiple papers and talks have been released covering this campaign, which used the ELIRKS backdoor when it was first discovered in 2012. It is known for using blogs and microblogging services to hide the location of its actual command-and-control (C&C) servers. This allows an attacker to change the C&C server used quickly by changing the information in these posts. Like most campaigns, BLACKGEAR has evolved over time. Our research indicates that it has started targeting Japanese users. Two things led us to this conclusion: first, the fake documents that are used as part of its infection routines are now in Japanese. Secondly, it is now using blogging sites and microblogging services based in Japan for its C&C activity.
